opening.headline: When you receive a notice about the end of support for a currently used model, you learn how to read the schedule and impact scope and connect to a fallback.
body: The model is not permanently available. The provider gradually discontinues the previous model by releasing newer, safer, and more performant models. If you need to determine where a particular model is being used upon receiving a notice email, your response will be delayed, and requests will fail once the retirement date has passed.

In this course, we examine the common structural approach that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google use to describe model lifecycles. We learn how to integrate key elements—decommissioning schedules, impact scope, and fallback models—into a unified framework for design. Finally, we follow a case study that walks through identifying affected services after receiving a notice and then working backward to calculate the response timeline.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the end-of-support policy and the role of fallback.
Support end dates can be aligned with service impacts and responses.

screens.title: Received notice of the Jeongjong's announcement, but the response is delayed.
screens.lead: When you select a number marker, you can view events occurring at each point in time on the timeline and the tasks you need to perform. Please check them in order from number 1.

visual.alt: A diagram showing three time points—notification received, just before termination, and after termination—across a timeline, each marked with a number indicator.

markers.label: Notice received
markers.title: The timestamp when the notice arrives
markers.body: Upon receipt of the notice, the responsible party verifies the target model ID, expiration date, and recommended replacement model. The provider notifies affected customers via email and posts the information in the documentation. At this point, the first action to take is to identify where within our services the model is being used; if there is no list of users, this process will consume significant time.

markers.label: Preparation period
markers.title: Preparation period from announcement to termination
markers.body: The duration of the preparation period varies depending on the provider and model type. During this period, alternative models should be evaluated, fallback options established, and a gradual transition implemented. Even if the period appears lengthy, reversing the calculation to determine the actual time required for evaluation and transition may reveal that there is actually little room for flexibility.

markers.label: End date
markers.title: On the day of expiration
markers.body: Anthropic's documentation states that requests for retired models are rejected. All users must complete the migration before the end date. If any users have not migrated by that time, service outages will occur.

markers.label: After termination
markers.title: After termination
markers.body: If code remains that calls the old model ID after termination, the request will fail and the user will encounter an error. At this point, it is already too late, so preparing a fallback model in advance is the final measure to reduce disruptions.

screens.outro: The question for this class is how to read termination policies and connect them to service impacts and fallbacks.

screens.title: Consider the end-of-support date for the currently used model
screens.lead: First, think about the questions on your own and then choose. There is no input or submission required; instead, what appears is a summary of the instructor's thoughts. Both questions are asking whether you can act immediately upon receiving the notice.

items.prompt: Can we see the model ID that our service is calling in one place?
items.answer: If the model ID is scattered across multiple codes and configurations, it takes a long time to locate its usage upon receiving a notice. If it can be viewed in a single list, the scope of impact can be immediately identified.

items.prompt: Who receives the termination notice, and where is it delivered?
items.answer: The provider notifies customers using that model via email. Notifications may not be delivered to individuals with personal accounts or former staff members. A designated process for both receiving the notification and forwarding it to the team must be established.

screens.outro: Now I will compare a table showing how the three vendors explain their model lifecycle.

screens.title: Common structure of termination documents for three service providers
screens.lead: The following table organizes the three vendors' documentation by aligning their descriptions of the model lifecycle and announcements in the same column. Compare the columns top to bottom to identify common structures.

data.caption: Model Lifecycle and Notification Methods by Provider
columns: Method to verify the end date
rows: Divided into four stages: Active, Legacy, Deprecated, and Retired. Deprecated means the feature continues to function but is not recommended, while Retired means requests fail.
Public models are notified via email and documentation at least 60 days prior to disposal.
Download model-specific and API key-specific usage data from the Console's Usage page to identify deprecated model usage locations.
List the recommended replacement models and retirement dates together in the table for each model.
Deprecation marks the beginning of the retirement process, and once retired, it has a defined end date. Models that are no longer updated are marked as legacy.
The general provisioning model lasts at least six months, the specialized variant at least three months, and the preview model can be as short as two weeks.
The `shutdown_date` field in the model list query is used to verify the expiration date within the program.
List the expiration date and recommended alternative model in one table.
Deprecation means announcing the discontinuation of support, while shutdown refers to the point when the endpoint is completely disabled and ceases to exist.
The end date is tracked in the table according to the earliest announced schedule, and models whose end dates have not yet been determined are shown as having no end date.
Check the table's expiration date in the release notes.
Release date, expiration date, and recommended replacement model are listed in one table. Some models automatically connect to subsequent models without expiring.
data.notes: All three documents share a common structure that presents their disposal schedule and recommended replacement models in a single table. Although the terminology may differ, once you identify the four key elements—stages, notification period, end date, and replacement model—you can read any provider's document in the same way.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the common structure, let's confirm the concept of combining schedule, impact scope, and fallback into one.

screens.title: Combine retirement schedule, impact scope, and fallback into one unit
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: The system for handling model deprecation consists of three components. First, Disposal schedule contains a schedule with the announcement date, deprecation date, and recommended replacement model, and calculates the preparation period by counting backward from the deprecation date. Second, sphere of influence identifies services, features, and customer segments associated with a given model, sorted by operational priority. Third, fallback model serves as a fallback model to be invoked when the primary model is unavailable, selecting candidates from the recommended replacement model list. Starting with the 4.6 generation of Claude, models without a date in their ID are designated as Fixed snapshot, and since they do not automatically update to the latest model, manual replacement is required. Models named with "preview" in their ID, such as preview model, can be notified briefly and thus must always have a fallback prepared for critical operations. When identifying usage scenarios, you can leverage the provider's Thank you for using it. functionality to verify the actual model being invoked.

terms.tip: Notice date, expiration date, and recommended alternative models are listed in the schedule. The start date is determined by reversing the calculation from the expiration date to account for the period required for evaluation and transition.
Services, features, and customer segments dependent on deprecated model IDs. It is safer to prioritize based on operational importance rather than call frequency.

This is a model that is called instead of the primary model when the primary model fails or terminates. Select a candidate from the recommended alternative model table and verify its quality with a quality assessment prior to the transition.

The model version pointed to by a model ID is a fixed model version. Anthropic provides a new version of the model under a new model ID without updating the weights or configuration of the existing model ID.
This model has "preview" in its name. OpenAI documents that such notifications may be issued as short as two weeks, and advises against using them for core operations.
This is how to find places using obsolete models by downloading and reviewing API key- and model-specific usage data from the Usage page of the Anthropic Console.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the system, let's follow an example case of identifying impacted services after receiving a notice.

screens.title: Case Explanation: Identifying Affected Services After Notification Receipt
screens.lead: The instructor explains the step-by-step response after receiving a disposal notice. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. The service configuration is assumed for illustrative purposes.

steps.title: See case
steps.body: A model deprecation notification email has arrived. This company offers three services: a customer inquiry chatbot, a summarization job, and an internal tool. It is still unknown which service uses the model being deprecated.

steps.title: Step 1: Convert the notice content into a table format
steps.body: Lists the target model ID, expiration date, and recommended replacement model in a table. This table becomes the basis for all subsequent steps. The remaining period from the expiration date to today is also included.

steps.title: Step 2: Conduct stakeholder investigation
steps.body: Search for the target model ID in code, configuration files, and environment variables. Then verify the actual model being called by reviewing usage audit logs. This approach can identify both cases where a model is used in practice but not in the code, and cases where a model is referenced in the code but never actually used.

steps.title: Step 3: Categorize Impact
steps.body: The chatbot in the user response path is prioritized highest, summary scheduling during off-hours is medium, and internal tools are lowest. Priority is determined by business importance rather than call volume.

steps.title: Step 4: Specify fallback
steps.body: Define alternative models and failover transition rules by service. The chatbot evaluates recommended alternative model candidates and selects one as the new primary model, designating another evaluated candidate as the fallback. Since the original model continues to operate until the end date, both configurations can be active during the transition period. Model IDs for dateless IDs introduced in generation 4.6 and later are not automatically updated, so direct model ID replacement is required. The same approach applies to summary deployments and internal tools. Thus, each service is defined with a primary model and a fallback pair.

steps.title: Step 5: Calculate the reverse schedule
steps.body: Calculate the start date for each service by reversing the period required for evaluation and transition from the end date. Start with the highest-priority chatbot first, and then proceed to preview models with shorter preparation periods. This approach helps avoid having to respond urgently right before the end date.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing the benchmarks obtained from the case study.

screens.title: The end date is input to the design.
screens.lead: Summarize the core of the lecture. Recall how to connect the initial question and termination policy with service impact and fallback when reading them.

paragraphs: Model support termination is not an exception but a regular occurrence. Therefore, termination dates should be treated as inputs to the design, not as events. When designing a service, you must know which model you depend on and what stage that model is currently in.

Each provider uses different status terms and notification periods. However, the structure of presenting four key elements—stage, notification period, expiration date, and recommended alternative model—in a table is consistent across providers. Once you identify these four elements, you can read any provider's documentation in the same manner.

Response involves organizing three elements: retirement schedule, impact scope, and fallback. The impact scope must be visible from a single location to enable quick identification, and service-specific fallbacks and transition schedules must be defined to prepare for end-of-life dates. Model IDs without dates do not automatically update, and preview models can be rolled out with short notifications.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: By predefining model ID lists, notification receipt paths, and service-specific fallbacks, you can begin responding immediately upon receiving a notification.

glossary.def: These are the provider's rules defining the model lifecycle stages and notification methods.
A model called instead when the primary model cannot be used.
This is a schedule containing the notice date, end date, and recommended alternative models.
The scope of services and features dependent on discontinued models.
This is the point at which the model is completely offline and cannot use the endpoint.

misconceptions.myth: Once it becomes deprecated, it cannot be used immediately.
misconceptions.fact: In Anthropic documentation, Deprecated means the model continues to operate but is not recommended, and once the end-of-life date passes and it becomes Retired, requests will fail.

misconceptions.myth: A model ID without a date is automatically updated to the latest model.
misconceptions.fact: 4.6 IDs without dates from generation four and later are fixed snapshots. New versions are provided with a new model ID and therefore require direct replacement.

misconceptions.myth: Termination notices are handled by the responsible party.
misconceptions.fact: If the recipient and destination lists are not predefined, the notification may not be delivered or may take a long time to locate destinations, resulting in delayed responses.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The end date is input from the design.
Although each provider uses different status terminology and notification periods, the structure of presenting schedules and alternative models in a table is the same.
Identify the impact scope and define fallbacks by service.
The start date is calculated by reversing the evaluation and transition period from the end date.

closing.reflection: When my service's model is down, where will the impact be felt, and what will the fallback mechanism be?
